newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch money curve remains flat, call rates high.
newsitem.headline: Dutch money curve remains flat, call rates high.

text.p: Dutch money market players said the current flat curve was attracting only few dealings and they said call money rates remained unnecessarily high.
"There is no tightness in the money market, but call money rates remain high," said one dealer.
Call was bid at around 2.81-2.88 percent. "This should come down to 2.75 percent," said one dealer, noting the Dutch special advances rate had been pegged at 2.50 for some time.
Dealers said the allocation of 2.86 billion guilders under the current special advances pact had not been too tight.
"Participants seem to be playing it safe and trying not to use too much of their credit quota," said one dealer.
Every three months the Dutch central bank sets a limit on the amount banks can borrow at the secured loans rate, currently 2.00 percent.
When banks try to build up savings under the scheme this can put upward pressure on call money.
Another dealer said a steeper curve would boost buying interest for the new Amsterdam Interbank Overnight Average (AIONA) product.
"The difference between call rates and six-month rates is so little that the attraction for AIONA is minimal. This would change if the curve becomes steeper," he said.
Dealers said they expected longer-dated money rates to remain stable for quite some time.
"Short-dated rates could come off though," said one.
The guilder was stronger versus the mark at 112.27 per 100 marks from 112.3125 on Monday.
